what: Virtualization (also called windowing) renders only the rows currently on screen plus a few extra, instead of every row in a huge list. The DOM stays small and the page stays fast, even with 100,000 items.
like: Like a film projector: the reel is miles long, but only the frame in front of the lamp is lit at any moment.
why: Thousands of DOM nodes make every style recalculation and interaction slow
Scrolling stays smooth because only about a screenful of rows is mounted
Memory and first render time stay flat as data grows

nodes.t: Full dataset|all rows, or paged cache

steps.t: Give the list a fixed viewport
steps.d: The scroll container has a set height and overflow: auto. The virtualizer needs to know how much room there is to fill.

With fixed row height, total height is count times height. With variable heights, it starts from an estimate and corrects as rows are measured. A spacer of that height makes the scrollbar behave normally.
On scroll, the virtualizer turns scrollTop into a start and end index.
A few extra rows above and below are rendered so fast scrolling does not show blank gaps. Too few gives flicker; too many wastes the saving.
Only that slice becomes DOM nodes, absolutely positioned (or translated) at the right offset. Rows leaving the window are unmounted or reused.
Set aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex, keep focus on a row that is scrolled away, and give a 'jump to' control since Ctrl+F cannot find unrendered rows.

choices.d: Pagination is simplest and keeps native find and accessibility. content-visibility: auto skips rendering off-screen sections with almost no code. Virtualize when you truly need one continuous scroll over thousands of rows.
Fixed heights are fast and exact. Dynamic heights (chat, cards with images) need measurement and cause scrollbar jumps; give a good size estimate.
TanStack Virtual is headless: it gives you ranges and offsets and you render the markup. react-window gives ready list and grid components. Headless is more flexible, components are quicker to start.
Small overscan saves DOM but risks blank flashes on fast flings; a few rows each side is the usual balance. Measure on a low-end phone.

instead.why: Controls how data arrives; virtualization controls how much is in the DOM
Classic pagination in the URL, with native find and simple accessibility

breaks.d: Rows are not rendered in time for the scroll position.
breaks.fix: Raise overscan a little, keep row render cheap, avoid heavy work in row components

breaks.d: Estimated heights differ from real ones, so total height changes while scrolling.
breaks.see: Thumb shifts or the list jumps
breaks.fix: Use a close estimate, measure rows once, or use fixed heights

breaks.d: A row unmounts when scrolled away, taking its input value or focus with it.
breaks.see: Typed text vanishes, keyboard focus resets
breaks.fix: Keep state in the parent or store, keep the focused row mounted, restore focus on return

say: Past a few hundred complex rows I virtualize: only the visible rows plus small overscan are in the DOM, so cost depends on the screen, not the data size.
I weigh it against pagination and content-visibility first, because virtualization breaks native find and needs extra accessibility work.
Row height is the key decision: fixed is simple and exact, dynamic needs measuring and a good estimate to avoid scrollbar jumps.

followups.q: How does it work with infinite scroll?
followups.a: Fetch pages with a cursor into a cache, and virtualize the combined list. Trigger the next fetch when the last rendered index nears the end, and cap pages in memory if the list is huge.
Use list or grid roles with aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex, keep keyboard focus stable, and offer search or jump-to since the browser cannot find rows that are not in the DOM.

today: Headless libraries such as TanStack Virtual (framework-agnostic: React, Vue, Solid, Svelte, Angular and more) are the common choice, with support for dynamic sizes, grids and end-anchored chat lists. CSS content-visibility: auto is now a cheap first step for moderate lists.
